title: Trump weighs new Iran strikes as Tehran sets seven conditions for nuclear talks
dek: Iran says it sent a nuclear proposal through Qatar but will not reopen Hormuz until its demands are met. Brent crude rose nearly 4% to $98.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
President Donald Trump met his national security team on Wednesday and Thursday to decide whether to resume full military operations against Iran, senior US officials told Fox News, as Tehran said it had sent Washington a nuclear proposal through Qatar but would not discuss it until seven conditions were met.

Oil, which had fallen sharply after Tuesday's US midterm elections on hopes of a deal, jumped again. Brent crude settled at $98.29 a barrel on Thursday, up nearly 4%, and US crude at $90.52, Fox News reported, after fresh attacks on tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz. For India, which relies on imported crude, that rebound undoes much of the relief of earlier in the week.

## What happened

Speaking in the Oval Office on Thursday, Mr Trump said: "I would rather not destroy the rest of the country if possible, but maybe I will have to. You'll know soon enough," according to Fox News. He also questioned whether the conflict was still a war, saying "there hasn't been anybody killed in many months", and said of Iran's nuclear programme: "They're not doing anything without our approval."

Axios, citing US officials, reported that he is weighing three options: new strikes, continuing to squeeze Iran's economy through the US naval blockade of its ports, or a deal that would include significant concessions. A US official told Axios that Central Command was finalising preparations to resume major combat operations but had not received a new order. US officials noted that the new moon on 9 November would mean little moonlight, conditions they described as favourable for military operations, Fox News reported.

Iran's top security official, Mohsen Rezaei, set out Tehran's position during a visit to Moscow, where he met President Vladimir Putin. "As long as they do not execute our seven conditions, we will neither open the Strait of Hormuz nor have negotiations," he said, according to Reuters. A senior Iranian official told Reuters that a nuclear proposal had been passed to the US through Qatar and that Washington was reviewing it. The full list of conditions has not been published; Reuters said they include the lifting of US sanctions, the release of frozen Iranian assets and war reparations. Washington has said nuclear issues must be part of any first round of negotiations.

## Attacks at sea

The fighting at sea did not stop. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Thursday that two oil tankers and a tugboat had caught fire in the strait and that another tanker had hit a mine east of it, CBS News reported; the Guards' accounts have not been independently confirmed. The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre separately reported that a tanker was hit by two unidentified projectiles about 50 nautical miles north of Madinat ash Shamal in Qatar. The crew's condition and the extent of the damage were not known.

Oman said it was still working with Iran on a joint mechanism to control traffic through the strait, which it said could "end the state of war", according to CBS News. Russia's foreign ministry told its citizens not to travel to Iran, citing the "risk of a new escalation".

## Background

The war began on 28 February, when the US and Israel attacked Iran; Iran struck back at Israel and at Gulf states that host US bases, and has since restricted shipping through Hormuz. A US strike on an anti-aircraft site on Iran's Qeshm Island on election night was the first in the area since June. Vice President JD Vance has blamed the war for the Republicans' midterm defeat and has urged an agreement, while Democrats, who won both houses of Congress, have said they could use spending bills to press for an end to it.

## What happens next

Mr Trump has said a decision will come soon. A third US aircraft carrier group, led by the USS Theodore Roosevelt, is due in Singapore on Friday and is not expected in the Middle East for at least two more weeks, a US official told CBS News; officials said the two carrier groups already in the region were sufficient. Qatari mediators are continuing indirect talks.
